Say which comparisons are legitimate and which is not, and why.

(5) Nine pupils have zero absences and eight exceed 50 days. Poisson
expects .0141 and .0074 in these bands; negative binomial expects 6.2136
and 7.3623. Explain what this adds to the coefficient and AIC
comparisons, and why there is no comparable quasi-Poisson probability

## Appendix A: Choice Sets and Cut-specific Structure {.unnumbered}

### What a nominal choice model assumes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

In a baseline-category multinomial logit, the probability ratio for two
categories depends on their two linear predictors. Adding a third
category changes the denominator of both probabilities, so it leaves
their ratio unchanged if those predictors stay fixed. This property is
called **independence of irrelevant alternatives** (IIA).

Imagine a travel choice between a car and a blue bus. If an otherwise
identical red bus becomes available, people who preferred the bus might
split between the two colours, leaving car use nearly unchanged. A model
that treats red and blue buses as independent alternatives instead
redistributes probability according to a more restrictive rule. The
problem is substantive similarity between alternatives, rather than a
minor numerical imperfection. The same question matters if two response
categories are nearly interchangeable or the available choice set
varies between people.

For labour-force participation, consider whether part-time and full-time
work are substitutes in the same way as not working and either work
category. The observed labels alone do not answer that question. IIA
checks and more flexible choice models can be useful, but a small-sample
formal test cannot establish a plausible choice mechanism. The nominal
fit in this chapter is a conditional description of the recorded
composition, with the stated working structure.

### A partial proportional-odds comparison {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The opinion example can be fitted through `MASS::polr()` or
`ordinal::clm()` using the same ordered response, rows, formula and logit
link. The coefficient vectors agree to numerical tolerance (within
$10^{-5}$ here), and both give AIC 10420.5924. Different function defaults
or reversed category order would prevent this direct comparison.


```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
bridge <- MASS::polr(poverty ~ religion + degree + country + age + gender,
                     data = opinion, Hess = TRUE)
AIC(bridge, po)
nominal_test(po)
```


Relaxing the country restriction allows a separate country comparison
at each cut point, while retaining common slopes for religion, degree,
age and gender. The fitted signs must be translated to the same
above-cut direction before comparison. @tbl-ch12-partial-full
reports that direction: a positive coefficient increases the log-odds
of a response **above** the named split, conditional on the remaining
variables. Australia is the reference country.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-ch12-partial-full
#| tbl-cap: "Country comparisons at the two cumulative splits, with common slopes for the remaining recorded predictors."
#| tbl-colwidths: [32,22,22,24]
ct <- coef(summary(cutfit))
cutrows <- grep("country", rownames(ct))
z <- ct[cutrows, , drop = FALSE]
term <- c("Norway, lower split", "Norway, upper split",
  "Sweden, lower split", "Sweden, upper split",
  "USA, lower split", "USA, upper split")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Comparison = term, `Above-cut coefficient` = -z[, 1],
  SE = z[, 2], `Odds ratio` = exp(-z[, 1]), check.names = FALSE),
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

The remaining coefficients and thresholds complete the partial model.
Thresholds retain the cumulative-link convention $\zeta_j-\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta$;
they receive no odds-ratio interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ch12-partial-common
#| tbl-cap: "Thresholds and common slopes in the partial proportional-odds fit."
#| tbl-colwidths: [45,18,18,19]
common <- ct[-cutrows, , drop = FALSE]
term <- c("Lower threshold", "Upper threshold", "Religion: yes versus no",
  "Degree: yes versus no", "Age per year", "Male versus female")
ratio <- c("---", "---", sprintf("%.4f", exp(common[3:6, 1])))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Parameter = term, Estimate = common[, 1],
  SE = common[, 2], `Odds ratio` = ratio, check.names = FALSE),
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

The likelihood-ratio comparison with the common-slope model is nested:
it frees three country contrasts at a second cut point. It gives
$\chi^2(3)=362.3463$, $p<.0001$, and reduces AIC from 10420.5924 to
10064.2461. This is evidence against a common country slope in this
specified model. Other restrictions and the observational interpretation
still require judgment. Allowing country to vary by cut does not
establish that every other term satisfies proportional odds.


```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
anova(po, cutfit)
AIC(po, cutfit)
```


The probability comparison below holds religion at "yes", university
degree at "no", age at 45 and gender at "female". The profiles define
what is being compared. They are not national population averages.
Probabilities are reported in the recorded order Too Little, About
Right, Too Much; inspect the changed allocation across all three,
rather than treating a threshold coefficient as a category probability.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-ch12-partial-probs
#| tbl-cap: "Profile probabilities under common and country-specific cumulative slopes."
#| tbl-colwidths: [19,24,19,19,19]
profile <- data.frame(religion = factor("yes", levels = levels(opinion$religion)),
  degree = factor("no", levels = levels(opinion$degree)),
  country = levels(opinion$country), age = 45,
  gender = factor("female", levels = levels(opinion$gender)))
a <- predict(po, newdata = profile, type = "prob")$fit
b <- predict(cutfit, newdata = profile, type = "prob")$fit
pr <- rbind(data.frame(Country = profile$country, Model = "Common slopes", a),
            data.frame(Country = profile$country, Model = "Cut-specific country", b))
names(pr)[3:5] <- c("Too Little", "About Right", "Too Much")
knitr::kable(pr, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

An adjacent-category logit instead compares neighbouring categories;
a continuation-ratio logit describes successive transitions conditional
on reaching a stage. Those models answer differently structured
questions. Category order is the starting point, but the response
process and the desired comparison determine which ordered model is
useful [@agresti2010].

## Appendix B: Residuals and Two-process Explanations {.unnumbered}

### Residuals and one influential record {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A Pearson residual divides the observed-minus-fitted difference by the
model's fitted standard deviation. A deviance residual gives a signed
contribution to discrepancy under the likelihood. Neither should be
read as an ordinary Normal residual merely because it is called a
residual. Discreteness and changing means shape both displays.


```{r}
#| label: fig-ch12-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals on each count model's own variance and likelihood scales."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels show Pearson and deviance residuals against fitted means for Poisson and negative-binomial fits. The pupil with 81 absent days is identified; the Poisson scale exaggerates the spread relative to its assumed variance."
#| fig-height: 6.0
#| fig-width: 6.2
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (model in list(mp, mn)) for (type in c("pearson", "deviance")) {
  rr <- residuals(model, type = type)
  plot(fitted(model), rr, pch = 16, col = "grey45", xlab = "Fitted days absent",
       ylab = paste(tools::toTitleCase(type), "residual"))
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  j <- which.max(absence$Days)
  text(fitted(model)[j], rr[j], "81 days", pos = 2, cex = .8)
  title(if (inherits(model, "negbin")) "Negative binomial" else "Poisson")
}
```


The largest absence count is 81 days. Removing that record asks a
sensitivity question; it does not establish that the record is an error.
Refitting without it should report the changed dispersion parameter,
the ethnicity interval and the continued need for a plausible variance
model. Automatic deletion would conceal the very upper-tail behaviour
the model is meant to explain.


```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
reduced <- subset(absence, Days < 81)
check <- MASS::glm.nb(Days ~ Eth + Sex + Age + Lrn, data = reduced)
check$theta
exp(confint.default(check)["EthN", ])
```


### When zero has a separate mechanism {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A pupil who was eligible to miss school but happened to attend every day
and a record that could never register an absence can both show zero.
The first belongs to the same count process as other pupils. The second
suggests a separate eligibility or recording process. Many zeros alone
do not distinguish them: an ordinary negative-binomial model can already
produce more zeros than a Poisson model with the same mean.

A **hurdle model** separates whether the count crosses zero from its
positive magnitude; its positive-count component is truncated at zero.
A **zero-inflated model** mixes a structural-zero component with an
ordinary count component that can itself produce zero [@mullahy1986;
@lambert1992]. These are different accounts of how records arise. An
extra zero parameter should be motivated by that account and checked
against its fitted consequences.

Comparisons with an ordinary count model can put mixture probabilities
on a boundary and can leave additional parameters unidentified under
the null. The usual interior chi-square likelihood-ratio reference is
therefore not automatic, nor is one universal half-and-half mixture
formula adequate for every such comparison. Specialist model-specific
methods or a carefully designed parametric bootstrap are needed before
attaching a calibrated p-value.

For further practice, explain why the quasi-Poisson fit cannot supply the
band-probability table, and carry out the 81-day sensitivity comparison.
In each case, distinguish what changes numerically from what still needs
a study-design or measurement justification.
